figures.caption: Figure 1: ClasSAE jointly learns a sparse dictionary and a class affinity matrix, enabling classifier-free class prediction and targeted editing: removing only the features exclusive to a class erases that class from the reconstruction while shared features are preserved.

Figure 2: Feature activation heatmaps for ClasSAE trained on DINOv3 patch tokens, using whole-image class labels only. Top: features claimed by “Siamese cat, Siamese.” Bottom: features claimed by “American Staffordshire terrier, Staffordshire terrier, American pit bull terrier, pit bull terrier.” Each panel reports the feature’s budget ki, its claim strength for the labeled class, and its mean activation. Details in Section F.

Figure 3: (a) Each dictionary coordinate holds a row of trainable class logits Λi (grey). A trainable vector κ splits a global association budget Ktot = ρd into per-feature budgets ki (orange), and Soft Top-ki turns each row into a claim Mi carrying exactly ki units of mass (green). Budgets need not be equal: row 1 is a specialist (k = 1), row 7 a generalist (k = 12), and what one row takes another must give up. (b) For a sample of class c, the SAE selects k̂ coordinates (blue) while column M:,c marks the coordinates that claimed c (green). The score is the fraction of the selected set that is claimed (shaded); the double arrow indicates that minimizing −sc pushes from both sides at once, since the encoder must rank claimed features into the top-k̂ while the table must claim features that actually fire. Both panels are drawn in the hard limit; during training S(x) and Fc are the soft weights π(x) and M:,c.

Table 1: Reconstruction quality. Comparison at matched target L0 ≈ 380. L0 is the realized L0-norm of the code; FVE is the fraction of input variance explained by the reconstruction; Alive is the fraction of dictionary coordinates that fire on at least one validation sample. Bold marks the best result among architectures matched to the target L0; †Top-AFA selects its own L0 and is excluded from this comparison.

Table 2: M -honesty. Mean/median cosine similarity (CS) and precision/recall/F1 between the train-side matrix (M for ClasSAE, post-hoc M̂ for baselines) and the test-side M̂ . ClasSAE variants demonstrate that M carries a real, class-faithful association, not just an artifact of training.

Table 3: Out-of-the-box classification. Acc, Acc Top 5, Acc Top 10: top-1, top-5, and top-10 accuracy. F1: macro F1. Margin: gap between the top two class scores. ClasSAE L1 is the top scorer on every metric, and all ClasSAE variants trained with true labels achieve a larger margin than any baseline. Standard is the strongest baseline: it outperforms the soft-gradient ClasSAE on accuracy and F1 and slightly exceeds ClasSAE Hard on Acc Top 10.

Table 4: Targeted probe perturbation. TPP at k ∈ {20, 200, 600} and under the PMI-graded edit (TPP PMI); Edit Strength is the mean L1 norm of the TPP PMI edit. ClasSAE Hard leads at k≥200 and ClasSAE L1 under TPP PMI, with the two smallest edit strengths.

Table 5: Joint-classifier unlearning. Graded-vs-shuffled forget-accuracy drop, retain-accuracy drop, and edit strength (mean L1 norm); the two drops are measured relative to baseline classifier accuracy. ClasSAE variants dominate on forget drop while keeping edit strength small.
